item.research_question: How can a quinary refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) be designed to exhibit high thermal stability and superior resistance to radiation damage (dislocation loops, cavities, and grain growth) under extreme irradiation environments compared to existing quaternary W-based alloys?
item.material_system: Quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA with compositions W29.4Ta42Cr5.0V16.1Hf7.5 (thin film) and W31Ta34Cr5.0V27Hf3.0 (thick film)
item.processing_route: Magnetron-sputtering deposition from metal targets (99.99% purity) at room temperature and 3 mTorr pressure with no bias voltage; power settings: W (200 W), Ta (400 W), Cr (50 W), V (350 W), Hf (25 W); film thicknesses: 100 nm (thin) and 3 µm (thick)
item.test_conditions: In situ TEM annealing at 1173 K for 30 mins; single-beam He implantation (16 keV) up to ~9% He; dual-beam irradiation (1 MeV Kr+ + 16 keV He+) to 8.5 dpa and ~9% He at 1173 K; ex situ Ar+ irradiation (400 keV) to 10 dpa at 1073 K; nanoindentation at 200 nm depth
key_findings: Average grain size of as-deposited sample was 24.5 ± 1.3 nm, increasing to 26.3 ± 1.1 nm after annealing at 1173 K.
Grain size increased to 36.3 ± 1.8 nm after He implantation, but refined to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm during dual-beam irradiation.
No dislocation loops were detected even after 8.5 dpa and 9.13% He implantation during dual-beam experiments.
Cavity formation saturated after 5 dpa and ~8.5% He, with total volume change of ~0.3% after 8.45 dpa.
Hardness of unirradiated thick film was 13.25 GPa, increasing to 16.25 GPa after annealing and 20 GPa after irradiation.
Hf segregated to grain boundaries after annealing but depleted from boundaries during irradiation.
No precipitation was observed in irradiated samples, unlike the quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA which showed Cr-V precipitation.
item.mechanism: Grain refinement under dual-beam irradiation is attributed to cascade effects where high-energy recoil events divide grains into sub-cascades near the initial grain size. The absence of precipitation and homogenization of elements is explained by the irradiation-induced ballistic mixing and the material's Order-Disorder Transition Temperature (ODTT) being close to the irradiation temperature, causing SRO parameters to approach zero. High irradiation resistance is due to high interstitial-vacancy recombination rates, lattice distortion, and the difficulty of defect clustering in the complex chemical environment.
item.limitations: The study acknowledges that further work is necessary to advance the technology readiness level, specifically regarding response to neutron irradiation, and that the effect of composition changes on mechanical strength requires investigation. Tensile measurements on coarse grain and bulk forms are also noted as necessary future steps.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the described design methodology can be utilized to devise and synthesize new RHEAs for different applications. They specifically state that the effect of SRO on the mechanical behavior of future RHEAs in extreme environments is a topic to be further explored, and that tensile measurements should follow on coarse grain and bulk forms.
quotes: Grain refinement occurred, and the average grain size dropped to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm after a total irradiation time of ~94 mins.
Dislocation loops were not detected even after 8.5 dpa and at 9.13% He implantation during the dual-beam experiment.
